chapter.title: The vanishing forest
chapter.body: In Paraguay's Chaco, north of Mariscal Estigarribia (Boquerón), forest turns into pasture in a matter of weeks. Ordinary satellite photos cannot see through clouds or the smoke from burning. Radar can.
chapter.why: We chose this area because clearing happened there during the period, it fits in a single NISAR image and it lies outside protected Indigenous territories.
chapter.stat_scenes_label: radar images from November 2025 to October 2026
chapter.stat_revisit_label: days between one pass and the next
chapter.stat_wave_label: is the radar wavelength: it goes through tree crowns

radar.title: Radar "listens" to the forest
radar.body: NISAR sends radio waves to Earth and measures the echo that comes back. In a forest, the wave bounces among branches and trunks and returns strongly in the HV channel. In a pasture it bounces once off the ground and barely comes back. So when the forest is cut, that echo drops.
radar.desc_hh: HH (ground signal): rises with rain and with piled trunks. On its own it can mislead.
radar.desc_hv: HV (forest signal): comes from the tree crowns. When the forest is cut, it drops a lot and does not come back. This is what we use to detect clearing.
radar.desc_ratio: HH/HV: the ratio between the two. It rises when the crowns are gone. We use it to color the radar view.
radar.illustrative: Typical example values, not measured in this area. dB measures echo strength: −3 dB is half.
radar.legend_title: How to read the radar view
radar.legend_fresh: Pink: recent clearing, with piled trunks
radar.driver_volume_body: No crowns, no bounces: the forest signal (HV) drops and does not recover. This is the footprint of clearing.
radar.driver_windrows_body: Trunks piled in rows give a strong HH echo for a few weeks.
radar.driver_fire_body: When those rows are burned, that echo goes away and bare soil is left.
radar.driver_moisture_body: Wet soil raises the HH signal. That is why we detect with HV and require two passes in a row before flagging clearing.

map.body: This is Paraguay on a simple map, with our study zones in dashed boxes, divided into hexagons. Red: radar-detected clearing. Purple: flood water in Ñeembucú, also estimated by radar. The stronger the colour, the more hectares. Pick a zone, press play or tap a hexagon.
map.ethics: We show radar-estimated changes in land cover, not whether they are legal. We use no cadastre and no owner names.

guide.title: How to read the map
guide.colors_body: We divided the study area into equal hexagons. Each hexagon where radar detected clearing is colored, and the color says how many hectares were cleared inside up to the chosen date. The pulsing ones grew in that pass.
guide.radar_body: It is not a photo: it is the image NISAR builds from the radar echo. Each color mixes two channels.
guide.chart_body: The blue line is the forest echo at each pass. If it falls below the red line and does not come back, the forest is gone.
guide.step1: Press play and watch the areas appear, pass after pass.
guide.step2: Tap a colored hexagon: the map zooms in and shows how much was cleared and when.
guide.step3: Switch to "Before / after" and drag the bar to compare two dates.

trust.title: We compare it with another satellite
trust.body: OPERA DIST-ALERT detects vegetation loss with optical satellites (Landsat and Sentinel-2): a different sensor and a different method. When both agree we gain confidence. When they do not, it can be clouds, smoke or our own error, and we show it anyway.

context.title: What happened before the radar
context.body: There was a story before NISAR. With US data we measured, inside each zone's box, how much forest was lost each year and how many fires there were, to tell clearing apart from fire.
context.stat_loss: of forest lost 2001–2024 ({pct}% of the forest in 2000)
context.flood_label: OPERA water images (Jun–Nov 2026) to validate the flood
context.chart_label: {zone}: hectares of forest lost and fire detections per year, 2001–2025
context.read_boqueron_norte: Almost no clearing until 2010, and its worst year was 2024: 16,000 ha lost with only 14 fire detections, so clearing, not fire. It is an active front, like the one the radar sees in 2025–2026. The fire record (2019) came one year after 11,000 ha were cleared in 2018: trees are felled first and the windrows burned later.
context.read_boqueron_sur: Cleared earlier: almost half of its forest of 2000 was lost, mostly between 2005 and 2014. Fires peak from September to November.
context.read_mbaracayu: The box holds the reserve and its surroundings. The loss peaks (2020 and 2024) match years with many fires: part of it is fire. In 2025 SENAD destroyed 134 ha of illegal cannabis crops inside the reserve (Agencia IP).
context.read_neembucu: A wetland zone: we do not measure clearing here. Fires are mostly grassland burning in August and September. For the October 2026 flood NASA has 156 OPERA DSWx-HLS and 53 DSWx-S1 images that could validate what the radar sees.
context.national_note: Country-wide figures by market year (USDA). Cattle drives clearing in the Chaco; soybean grows mostly in the Eastern Region, under the zero-deforestation law.
context.sources: Sources: UMD Global Forest Change 2000–2024 (forest with 30% canopy or more), NASA FIRMS MODIS (fire detections), NASA OPERA DSWx, USDA FAS PSD. Our own counts over each zone's box; forest loss includes clearing and fire. Details in docs/CONTEXT.md.

next.title: A radar that never gets tired
next.body: NISAR looks at the whole planet every 12 days, day and night, through clouds and smoke. This is what can be built with it.
next.use_alerts_body: With the same method over the whole Chaco, an alert can reach environmental officers in weeks, not months.
next.use_trace_body: Knowing when a place changed helps supply chains show they buy from land without recent clearing.
next.use_wetlands_body: Radar also sees water under vegetation: it can follow floods like the one in Ñeembucú in July 2026.
limits: The date is the date of the satellite pass: ±12 days, or more after a missing pass (we say so).
We only see clearings of 5 hectares or more.
Most data is provisional and the last date is validated: we adjust every date so they can be compared.
We only look at what was forest on a 2021 map (ESA WorldCover) and that radar also saw as forest at the start.
Rain and fire move the signal: that is why we require two out of three passes in a row.
Hexagons summarize the clearings: the 1 km detail is under "More options".
We say nothing about whether a clearing is legal: that needs cadastre and permits we do not use.
steps: Interferometry (GUNW) to date each clearing more precisely.
Polarimetric decomposition to separate trunks, soil and crowns.
Comparison with Sentinel-1 (C-band) to show why L-band matters.
Machine learning trained on optical alerts.

zones.label: Study zone
zones.note_water: Flooding zone (chapter 2): open water and flooded vegetation estimated by radar at each date, in purple hexagons. No clearing detection.
zones.note_control: Control zone (chapter 3): the Mbaracayú Reserve and its surroundings, under the zero-deforestation law. It is not a disaster: it checks that the method raises no false alarms in protected forest. The box also holds cropland and earlier forest loss, so anything red here is a detection to review.
